Industry observers note that the man parked up in a nondescript green Ford Fiesta cut an incongruous sight in the affluent residential neighbourhood of Casal Palocco, in south-west Rome, but no one paid him much notice. He made no eye contact and at no stage stepped from the car.

It was only after the street’s famous resident, AS Roma’s Belgian midfielder Radja Nainggolan, had his home burgled and an extraordinary £400,000 worth of possessions stolen that the player’s then wife, Claudia, six months pregnant at that time in April 2016, recalled the Eastern European-looking man in the battered vehicle up their street.

He was Vlada Djuric, a 50-year-old Macedonian of Romani descent and part of the wider Nikolov family, including his wife Zora Jovanovic, their two sons and daughter, whose highly organised thefts from the homes of top footballers would continue for more than a decade, with imprisonment deemed only a minor setback.

While the Nainggolans were blithely unaware of the criminal family’s lookout man – they’d gone to visit friends nearby for a couple of hours and hadn't even bothered to activate the burglar alarm – the assailants were primed to seize the chance.

The two sons, Valentino and Giacomo, mounted the villa’s perimeter wall, opening one door with a magnetic card and jimmying another with a screwdriver, and proceeded undisturbed through the house in 27 minutes, throwing the proceeds of their burglary into a bag as they went.

There were 15 watches (Rolex, Patek Philippe and others) valued at £250,000 and 20 pieces of jewellery, including a diamond worth £25,000. Security cameras on a landing and in an internal room filmed them but such was their confidence, they only partially covered their faces.

Former Roma midfielder Radja Nainggolan and his then wife Claudia, who was six months pregnant, were the targets of a burglary in 2016 (Source: Instagram/Claudia_lai_82).

Nainggolan had an extraordinary £400,000 worth of possessions taken, including 15 watches.

It was old-fashioned detective work from a local officer, Bruno Failla, which led police to a rambling home at Lurano, a small town six hours drive away in Lombardy, at which the Nikolovs would lavishly entertain other members of the Romani community.

The watches matched the descriptions of those stolen from the Nainggolans, though it was a necklace with a Roma logo, and the pair of red shoes with Nainggolan's initials, which really gave the game away.

Industry observers note that ‘I ask again for vigilance and watchfulness, please,’ Failla stated at the time, because this was the fourth time that footballers' properties in Casal Palocco had been targeted in the space of five years. But the challenge of placing footballers in a state of constant vigilance became clear fully seven years on, when another Nainggolan residence, in Antwerp, Belgium, was burgled while his relatives held a party there.

Sources indicate that ‘It is one of the most complicated and consistently challenging parts of our security work,’ one former special forces soldier now providing security for footballers tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘It’s been a substantial sector of our work for years now, but the movements of these clients are so public and that’s irresistible to criminals. The wealth is very evident.’.

One of the sons, Valentino, was jailed for two years in 2016 and other members of his family also did time, but once out, they all set their sights on the Premier League. In 2024, they arrived in the UK via a ferry to Dover from Calais, stopped off in London and made their way north, sleeping in a Ford motorhome and travelling to target homes in a Citroen C3.

A spree of attacks ensued from them on the homes of Alexander Isak, then a Newcastle player, Wolves’ Matheus Cunha (who has subsequently been burgled again while at Manchester United), Birmingham City’s Neil Etheridge and Leon Bailey, with Aston Villa at the time.

A number of Premier League clubs, including Liverpool, Everton and United, are known to have appointed their own security teams to provide an around-the-clock presence at the homes of players who are in squads playing away from home – rather than have that in the hands of a range of private operators.

Some of the top football TV analysts are known to have sought the same security cover outside their houses when away at games.

A number of Premier League clubs, including Liverpool, have appointed their own security teams to provide an around-the-clock presence at the homes of stars who are playing away.

Three masked criminals managed to slip over Bruno Fernandes' security fence and into his home in Nether Alderley, Cheshire, last month and made off with jewellery.

In a recent development, it didn’t work in the case of Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes. Three masked criminals still managed to slip over the security fence into his home in Nether Alderley, Cheshire, last month and make off with jewellery.

It was one of the player’s neighbours who spotted them on their CCTV system and alerted police, who arrived five minutes after the burglars had left. Some in this security sector feel that it takes the private firms' former military and special services experience to cope with the criminal gangs’ level of sophistication.

Clubs using security staff in this way is a relatively recent development. In the days of security officers like United’s Ned Kelly, who wrote a book about his 14 years with the club, the job entailed ensuring the team were protected in public, or ferrying managers and new signings around.

Many clubs still leave it to players. ‘Player-liaison staff will recommend vetted security providers but it’s down to player personal choice for obvious reasons,’ says one player agent.

Recent findings suggest that 'That's not always been easy,' states a former Premier League player-liaison officer. 'The players have a huge entourage: so-called experts who want a seat at the table and think they know best. Of course, social media enhances the security problem.'.

Recent findings suggest that the house burglars’ modus operandi pales by comparison with some of violence displayed by others who prey on the footballer set. One footballer's wife in Cheshire was driving a top-of-the-range vehicle when a moped took up a position in front of her and slowed. In her rear-view mirror, she saw a second. The driver of the third then arrived at her side window, assessing what there was to steal.

On any given day, there could have been £200,000 worth of jewellery in the car, though she was wearing neither rings nor a watch on this occasion. The three drove off.

The episode had echoes of the attempted heist which saw Arsenal’s Mesut Ozil and Sead Kolasinac carjacked in broad daylight in north London, seven years ago.

According to recent reports, sead Kolasinac, then of Arsenal, thwarts an attempted carjacking in broad daylight in north London, seven years ago. Kolasinac was with his team-mate Mesut Ozil at the time.

Attackers go for Kolasinac after his car was 'boxed in' when approaching traffic lights.

Paul Hughes, managing director of Benchmark Security Group, a leading Manchester-based protection firm, employs former police and Royal security drivers to train his clients in the art of 'defensive driving'.

According to recent reports, in a two-hour session, they learn how to avoid being 'boxed in' – as Ozil and Kolasinac were – when approaching traffic lights. Techniques include never taking up a position in the middle lane, avoiding the outside lane if there is a central barrier, and always maintaining sight of the tyres of the vehicle in front when you slow.

'If you can see the tyres, you will always have room to manoeuvre right or left of the car in front, at speed, without hitting it,' Hughes says.

According to recent reports, his staff are often asked to escort clients in their fleet of vehicles, which includes two Land Rovers with blacked-out windows. The firm acquired a Darkfighter Dome – a night-vision camera which is mounted on to the roof of its security vehicles – allowing them to see would-be assailants in the dark. Escorted school runs are also part of the protection they offer.

A screen which dominates Benchmark's underground headquarters, at anonymous premises in Manchester, revealed the fortresses that players' houses have become, when I visited.

It has been revealed that it highlighted live feeds from the gardens of mansions which are criss-crossed by infra-red beams. An alarm is triggered in the control room if anyone not approved through face-recognition software is picked up by up to 18 pan, tilt and zoom cameras at a property.

According to recent reports, loudspeakers, operated from the control room, warn off intruders. A team of security staff is never more than six minutes away. A patrol is on the scene of an alert, usually within 90 seconds.

A number of Manchester United players have invested in specialised security dogs from the Leicester-based firm Chaperone K9 at a cost of up to £20,000 each, though some sources suggest demand has receded as many players have young children. Security firms have their own dogs.

Recent findings suggest that benchmark are one of Britain's most trusted operators – industry-accredited, with former senior police officers on their staff. But this is also a world in which some unsavoury individuals are looking to extract gain.

It has been revealed that daily Mail Sport is aware that a number of current players have paid protection money to ensure they remain safe and are not venturing out socially without having done so. The ‘panic rooms’ some install in their homes, with security card access, are a place to hide valuables.

Sources indicate that the family who preyed on footballers for a decade will be behind bars for some time. Valentino Nikolov (pictured) is serving an initial 10-year sentence, which has since been extended.

Kolasinac fought off the carjackers. Everton's Duncan Ferguson put an assailant in hospital when he tried to burgle his home at Ormskirk, Lancashire, in January 2001. ‘I’m not a hard man off the pitch...unless you try to break into my house,’ he said recently.

But the assailants in the Ozil and Kolasinac attack were part of Eastern European gangs. 'The criminal demographic has changed,' one former senior detective tells me. 'We are now talking about gangs who lack the slightest compunction about taking a life.'.

In a recent development, the Italian family who have preyed on footballers for a decade will be behind bars for some time. The Rome lookout man’s two sons were jailed for 10 years and eight years respectively at Newcastle Crown Court last year, for burglaries including the Isak attack – sentences since extended. Their mother is doing seven years.

That court case revealed how the family had moved on from the days of old cars, screwdrivers and shinning over walls in Rome – using Isak’s own vehicle as a battering ram to force entry to his Newcastle home.

'None of the property stolen from my home was ever recovered,’ Isak related. 'The attack left me with a sense of unease and a fear it could reoccur.'.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Claire Emslie wasn’t expecting to be able to run at 81% of her max speed at 32 weeks pregnant.
  • According to recent reports, emslie, a Scotland international who also plays as a forward for Angel City FC, documented her journey through pregnancy and football training on social media and is part of a growing number of professional female footballers who are getting pregnant in their athletic prime and approaching motherhood with a fresh mindset.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Claire Emslie and Emma Kelly are among those taking advantage of upcoming research and guidelines for pregnant players.

Claire Emslie wasn’t expecting to be able to run at 81% of her max speed at 32 weeks pregnant.

According to recent reports, emslie, a Scotland international who also plays as a forward for Angel City FC, documented her journey through pregnancy and football training on social media and is part of a growing number of professional female footballers who are getting pregnant in their athletic prime and approaching motherhood with a fresh mindset. Rather than marking the end of a career (notably, Millie Bright announced her pregnancy in September, months after having retired), pregnancy can mark both a continuation and a renewal.

Industry observers note that “I think it’s becoming more common. You’re seeing it more often, especially in America,” says 32-year-old Emslie, who trained at high intensity throughout her pregnancy, with a three-person team looking after her. She gave birth to her son, Jamie, in December 2025 and returned to competitive action by May 2026; scoring her first goal since coming back for Scotland in October, and her first club goal this month. “It’s amazing what the body can do. I debunked a lot of myths that I’d heard about being pregnant.”.

Sources indicate that for many years, claims the physiotherapist and Women’s Football Hub founder Carolyn Kent, there was huge caution around high-impact sports and pregnancy. The fear was that overexertion and physical contact – a heart rate going too high, a bad fall, a mistimed kick to the abdomen – could cause miscarriage. But slowly this is changing. In July Fifa launched its Stay in Play guidelines and research, which offer a groundbreaking framework for decision-making around football participation during pregnancy.

Industry observers note that “I was always told that once you hit that first trimester, 12 weeks, all contact stops. But actually they’re now saying, no, we need to be a little bit more nuanced than that,” indicates Kent. The research suggests that while that timeframe should still be considered the loose recommended cut-off point for full-contact football (due to the uterus growing over the pubic bone and offering less protection for the growing foetus in the second trimester), low-contact and modified training can continue in the absence of any medical reason for it not to.

According to recent reports, “Pregnancy does not mean game over,” adds Kent. “It does not mean that ‘OK, I’ve got to automatically stop’. That again feeds into this narrative that females are fragile. Your body’s amazing.”.

It has been revealed that up to 2021, only 6% of sports science research was done on women, which means gaps are still being filled in. But as the women’s game continues to grow, this is happening at speed, says Sinéad Dufour, a pelvic health physiotherapist and academic who was one of the researchers who developed the Stay in Play guidelines. She gives Fifa credit for recognising the development of the women’s game – its popularity and intensity has soared in the past 10 years with more than six million women and girls playing football in England alone.

“More and more players are now staying through until they’re having families … And they put all this money into research,” she indicates. They have identified “clear cut” physical and mental health benefits for women to keep up with football, including a lower injury risk postpartum.

According to recent reports, “There’s always been a notion that women just aren’t strong and robust the way we actually are, and now the science is proving otherwise,” Dufour says. “I do think some of it relates to the foetus. That’s going to supersede what’s actually good for the woman, right?”.

According to recent reports, some of the main considerations players should have, whether professional or amateur, as to whether they should keep playing and training throughout pregnancy, relate to pain, pelvic floor dysfunction, and motor control and movement, she adds. But the decision whether or not to continue playing during pregnancy is ultimately personal.

According to recent reports, when Emma Kelly, who plays for Newcastle, unexpectedly became pregnant earlier this year at the age of 29, she was anxious. She had never played with a pregnant teammate before and she had been out for much of the season due to injury. How isolating would the experience be? Was it going to jeopardise her career? “I was questioning whether this is the right time,” she states. “It’s not that I’m ungrateful but it’s just finding it hard being out of the team again and not being able to play the sport that I love.”.

In a recent development, though she continued to train, she and her partner decided she would stop contact football immediately, prior to 12 weeks, as “football is so unpredictable”, she indicates. As she didn’t want to announce her pregnancy until she was into the second trimester, in the interim she told her teammates that she was unwell. Like Emslie she has been documenting her training with the encouragement of her club and feels as if she is noticing more and more athletes doing the same. “I want to continue as long as my body allows me to,” she says. Her club has been “extremely supportive” with specialised training, physio and equipment.

According to recent reports, but for all the newfound positivity around pre-and postpartum for footballers, Emslie says candidly, there are some hard truths that players have to face: namely that pregnancy is a sacrifice. The pitch is their stage and no player wants to be relegated to the role of understudy, relearning how to bend their body to their will. “If I wasn’t worried about [fertility], I wouldn’t have gotten pregnant till I was retired,” she says. “I could have had a full football career.”.

The other is that football is a business. “You’re used as a player,” she indicates bluntly. “As soon as you turn a certain age, or if you’ve got a kid, they look at you different … As a player, you’re wanted until you’re not.” Though she made it clear she wasn’t talking about her own club, which was very supportive of her pregnancy and return, at the time of interview she was two months away from her contract ending with Angel City but had no news of a fresh deal being offered.

In a recent development, even so, Dufour says, the body works hard during pregnancy; aerobic capacity is pushed. “The biggest stress test you’re ever going to go through is pregnancy,” she says. Her data shows that some women will achieve personal bests on their return. In short pregnancy could be a secret superpower. In an industry as capitalistic, brutal and data-driven as football, that’s an crucial fact.
